Sweep Backtest (SBT)

6300 optimizer configurations over one FIXED curation (data/cbt_3yr_v4) · no LLM, no re-curation · knobs from investor_profile.backtest.md

1. Parameter settings

The 6 FREE swept knobs — every combination is a cell, 4×3×7×3×5×5 = 6300 configs — and the values considered. These knobs only RE-WEIGHT a fixed set of curator picks, which is what makes the grid free: no LLM call is made and no event is discovered or closed differently. Every other optimizer / curator parameter is held at its investor_profile.backtest.md value.

parametervalues sweptcurrent (profile)
max_watchlist4, 6, 8, 128
concentration_cap0.25, 0.4, 0.60.25
lookback_period_days7, 10, 14, 21, 30, 45, 6014
drop_unfunded_weeks0, 2, 40
risk_aversion0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.04.0
min_trade_size0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.30.2

2. Return vs drawdown

The horizontal axis is max drawdown — the book's biggest peak-to-trough loss as a fraction of its running peak; further right = deeper loss. The vertical axis is annualized return, so upper-left is best. Each point is one config; colour is the share of the winners' gains handed back by the losers, so a pale point in the upper-left is the whole objective at once. The live config is the purple ★ star.

3. Return vs L1 churn

Same points, risk axis replaced by L1 churn = annualized one-way turnover (Σ|Δweight| across rebalances, ×100/yr): how much of the book is traded per year. Weights are held flat between rebalances, so drift never counts as a trade. Trading is free in an IRA, so read this as stability, not cost: lower churn = less noise-chasing and less overfit, making upper-left the sweet spot. Colour is Sharpe: a dark point at high churn is trading that actually pays for itself.

4. Return vs L2 course correction

Same idea, but the path length the book was dragged through weight-space (√ΣΔweight² per rebalance, summed and annualized). Against L1 it weights concentrated single-name rotations more heavily. The useful read is whether the two norms rank configs alike — if they do, the churn ordering is robust rather than an artefact of which norm was picked. Coloured by Sharpe, as panel 3.

5. Return vs Sharpe

The same cloud with Sharpe on the horizontal — return per unit of volatility, the measure table 6 actually ranks by. This is the one panel here where upper-RIGHT is best, since higher Sharpe is better; every other risk axis on this page reads the other way. Colour is max drawdown, pinned to the same 20–120% band as panel 6 so the two are comparable. The cloud is a tight rising diagonal — return and Sharpe correlate +0.92 across the grid, so for most configs they say the same thing and there is no return/risk trade to agonise over. The divergence is all in the tail, which is exactly where a config gets picked. On this book the grid's biggest final value ($1.52M, 225%/yr) ranks only 1,351st of 6,300 by Sharpe — 79th percentile — because it earns that return on a 59% drawdown. The best-Sharpe cell (1.93) makes $401K on a 24% drawdown instead. Read the top-right corner, not the top edge: a point that is high but far left is return bought with volatility a live account has to actually sit through.

6. Return vs cancellation

The fourth view of the same points, and the one that matters most: the horizontal axis is the share of the winners' gains handed back by the losers, so upper-left is best — a book that earns and keeps it. Colour is max drawdown, so a pale upper-left point earns well, keeps it, and does so without a deep hole. The cloud's shape is itself the finding: if it were a tight rising diagonal these knobs would only be trading return against cancellation, and it is not one.

7. Recommended settings

The shortlist: every config that clears all four gates — read off panels 2, 4, 5 and 6 — max DD < 35% · L2 < 800/yr · Sharpe > 1.2 · cancelled < 25% — 414 of 6,300 survive, ranked by Sharpe. The bars were re-cut 2026-08-15 and are far tighter than the set they replace (DD < 65, L1 < 1800, L2 < 1100, cancelled < 60, which left 4,368 standing). Each does real work alone: DD keeps 26.9% of the grid, Sharpe 20.6%, cancellation 26.6%, L2 53.0%. L1 is dropped — L2 is the stricter of the two churn norms here, so gating both was redundant. The earlier note that there was "deliberately NO churn gate, because median Sharpe rises monotonically with churn" was true of an older book and has since inverted: on this one median Sharpe peaks in the L2 600–800 band (1.03) and collapses above it (0.97 by 1,000, 0.63 by 1,400, 0.45 beyond), while median drawdown climbs 35% → 76%. An L2 ceiling of 800 sits exactly on that peak. plateau = ½·the config's own cancellation + ½·the mean of its grid neighbours, so a lone in-sample spike with weak surroundings still shows up. A ★ marks the survivor that is best on that column (plateau, cancellation, annualized return, Sharpe). Those four stars rarely land on one row — where they scatter IS the trade-off, and a config carrying two of them is the honest compromise. Top 30 shown; the rest expand below. Current live config on the last row.

8. risk_aversion × lookback_period_days

Median cancellation at each combination of the two knobs whose marginals span the widest range. This is the panel a 1-D sweep cannot produce, and it is where the interactions hide — a value that looks harmless on average can be the worst choice in one corner of the grid.

9. Each knob on its own

For every value of every knob: the MEDIAN cancellation across all cells holding that value (the bar) and the BEST single cell (the dot). A wide gap between them means the knob only pays in combination with something else. The live setting is outlined.

10. Portfolio value vs max_events

The one knob on this page that is not free to sweep. Everything above replays a FIXED curation through different book math, so 6,300 cells cost nothing; max_events decides which events stay live and so which tickers ever reach the optimizer, meaning each point here is a full re-curation ($0.00 and several hours for the series). Bars are final portfolio value, the line is the share of events culled at birth — opened and retired without a single agent read, i.e. work paid for and thrown away. Read the CULL LINE first: it is a structural count the cap moves directly, while final value is one lucky name away from noise, and each point is a single stochastic sample (the scout is an LLM; two runs at the same cap would differ). A monotone trend across the six is worth something; a one-point spike in dollars is not.

11. Risk-adjusted quality vs max_events

Sharpe per cap, with the shortlist's > 1.2 floor drawn in. This is the panel to weigh against 10, because Sharpe is what table 7 actually ranks by and what the live config was chosen on — a cap that wins on final value while dropping below the floor has not won anything we would deploy. Bars under the line are configs the shortlist would refuse regardless of how much money they made.

12. Where the money sits, and what it gives back

Three percentages on ONE axis, all of them defects: max drawdown (the hole the book digs), cancellation (winners' gains handed back by losers) and idle days (days holding NO position at all — the cash band in CBT plot 9). Dashed lines are the shortlist bars, DD < 35% and cancellation < 25%. Idle days is the one that ties this knob to the optimizer: a tight cap starves the watchlist, so the book sits in cash not because the curator ran out of theses but because it was never allowed to open them. All three are better LOW, so a cap whose three bars are all short is the one to want.

13. What the cap costs, and what it buys

Left bars: the LLM bill for that curation — the only thing on this page that is not free, since each point is a full re-curation rather than a replay. Right bars: the same money divided by tickers that actually got funded, which is the efficiency question — a cap that opens hundreds of events the optimizer never funds is paying the event-agent bill for reading it may as well not have done. Only the agent half of the bill scales with the cap; the scout reads the same ticker-groups either way, which is why the left bars flatten while the cap keeps rising.
